Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- While all eyes seem to be on "Slumdog Millionaire" for the Oscars, one very courageous little girl will be focused on another India-based film at the ceremony. Pinki, like millions in developing countries, had to live with her deformity and suffer the social consequences. It's called "Smile Pinki," and it's up for an Oscar, too -- nominated for best short documentary, which it won on Sunday. The little girl watching it from inside the Oscar ceremony has traveled all the way to Los Angeles, California, from her small Indian village with her dad -- and it has been an incredible journey for Pinki Sonkar. "Smile Pinki" tells the story of her transformation from a sad outcast to a vibrant 8-year-old with plenty of spunk. Pinki was born with a cleft lip, and her impoverished family did not have the money for corrective surgery. Like millions of other children born with the lip deformity in developing countries, Pinki simply had to live with it and suffer the social consequences. Her father Rajendra Sonkar says: "She used to go to school and the kids would not befriend her. She would say, 'I don't want to go to school.'"  Watch how Pinki was transformed by the operation » . "Pinki was a depressed, sad, lonely, shy, young little girl, growing up on the periphery of the society in a little village," said Satish Kalra, director of Smile Train's South Asian region, after meeting with Pinki. The little girl's own family was ashamed of her, Kalra says. But all of that has changed. Pinki is now a real pistol, full of energy and confidence, and she has a fantastic smile too -- thanks to the Smile Train charity. Smile Train teaches doctors in their own countries to operate on cleft lips, a deformity afflicting up to four million children across the world. iReport: Share your Oscar predictions . Pinki just happened to be one of the chosen candidates for surgery and was also chosen to be the subject of the documentary. The film chronicles her transformation, following her from her village to the hospital and home again. "She has absolutely and totally changed," said Pinki's surgeon, Dr. Subodh Kumar. The film's director is Megan Mylan. She has won several awards but not an Oscar -- until now. For Pinki and her dad, being able to see the film's director win an Oscar would be a thrill. But they know they already have the greatest prize: Pinki's new smile. "I am so happy that my daughter's lips have been repaired," her dad Rajendra said with a smile, expressing hope that the movie will inspire people to help children whose families can't afford the surgery.

**(CNN) —** While much of the attention at the Oscars seemed focused on *Slumdog Millionaire*, one remarkably courageous little girl had her sights set on another film based in India.

*Smile Pinki*, nominated for—and on Sunday awarded—the Oscar for Best Documentary Short, tells the story of Pinki Sonkar’s transformation from a sad, ostracized child into a spirited and vibrant 8-year-old.

Pinki traveled with her father from their small Indian village to Los Angeles, California, to attend the Oscar ceremony—an extraordinary journey for both of them.

Born with a cleft lip, Pinki came from an impoverished family that could not afford corrective surgery. Like millions of children with the deformity in developing countries, she was forced to live with it and endure the resulting social consequences.

Her father, Rajendra Sonkar, recalled: “She used to go to school and the kids would not befriend her. She would say, ‘I don’t want to go to school.’”

**Watch how surgery transformed Pinki »**

“Pinki was a depressed, sad, lonely, shy young little girl, growing up on the periphery of society in a little village,” said Satish Kalra, director of Smile Train’s South Asia region, after meeting her. According to Kalra, even Pinki’s own family was ashamed of her.

But all of that has changed. Pinki is now a real pistol—energetic, confident and full of spirit—and she has a wonderful smile, thanks to the Smile Train charity.

Smile Train trains doctors in their own countries to perform cleft-lip surgery, addressing a deformity that affects as many as four million children worldwide.

**iReport: Share your Oscar predictions**

Pinki happened to be selected both as a candidate for surgery and as the subject of the documentary. The film chronicles her transformation, following her journey from her village to the hospital and back home again.

“She has absolutely and totally changed,” said Pinki’s surgeon, Dr. Subodh Kumar.

The film was directed by Megan Mylan, who had won several awards but had never received an Oscar—until now.

For Pinki and her father, seeing the film’s director win an Oscar was a thrill. Yet they know they have already received the greatest prize: Pinki’s new smile.

“I am so happy that my daughter’s lips have been repaired,” Rajendra said with a smile, expressing hope that the film will inspire people to help children whose families cannot afford the surgery.

*Smile Pinki*, which received the Oscar for best short documentary on Sunday, follows Pinki Sonkar’s remarkable journey. The 8-year-old and her father traveled from their small village in India to Los Angeles, California, to attend the ceremony.

Born with a cleft lip, Pinki came from a family too poor to pay for corrective surgery. Like millions of children with the condition in developing nations, she was forced to endure both the physical deformity and the social stigma surrounding it.

Her father, Rajendra Sonkar, recalled that other children refused to make friends with her at school. Pinki would tell him that she no longer wanted to attend.

After meeting her, Satish Kalra, Smile Train’s regional director for South Asia, described Pinki as a withdrawn, unhappy, isolated, and timid child living on the margins of village society. According to Kalra, even members of her own family felt embarrassed by her.

The condition affects as many as four million children worldwide.

Pinki was selected to receive the surgery and was also chosen as the focus of the documentary. The film traces her experience from her village to the hospital and then back home, capturing her change from a sorrowful outcast into a lively young girl.

Her surgeon, Dr. Subodh Kumar, said the transformation was absolute and complete.

The documentary was directed by Megan Mylan, who had earned several honors before receiving her first Academy Award. Pinki and her father were excited by the possibility of watching Mylan win the Oscar, but they believed they had already received the most valuable reward: Pinki’s repaired smile.

Rajendra said he was overjoyed that his daughter’s lip had been corrected. He also expressed hope that the film would encourage people to support children whose families cannot afford the necessary surgery.

**From stigma to a new smile: How cleft-lip surgery changed Pinki Sonkar’s life**

**MIRZAPUR, India —** Born with a cleft lip in a poor village in northern India, Pinki Sonkar spent her early childhood facing stares, teasing and isolation. Her family could not afford the surgery that could repair the congenital condition, and for years, Pinki’s future appeared limited by a difference that was visible every time she smiled.

Then, a chance encounter changed her life.

A social worker identified Pinki in Uttar Pradesh’s Mirzapur district and connected her family with a program offering free cleft surgery. She traveled to Varanasi, where surgeon Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh repaired her lip at a hospital supported by the cleft-care charity Smile Train.

The operation, performed when Pinki was about 5 years old, took only a fraction of a day. Its effects stretched far beyond the operating room.

Pinki was able to eat and speak more easily, attend school with greater confidence and interact with other children without the same level of ridicule. For her family, the surgery opened possibilities that once seemed out of reach.

Her journey became the focus of **“Smile Pinki,”** a 39-minute documentary directed by American filmmaker Megan Mylan. The film follows Pinki and another child, Ghutaru, as they travel from rural communities to receive cleft surgery. It captures their families’ uncertainty, the medical procedure and the emotional moment when they return home transformed.

“Smile Pinki” won the **Academy Award for best documentary short subject in 2009**, bringing international attention to Pinki and to the challenges faced by children with untreated clefts.

A cleft lip occurs when facial tissue does not fully join during pregnancy. In many cases, surgery can repair the opening and improve a child’s ability to eat, speak and breathe. But in low-income and rural communities, families may lack access to specialists or may not know that treatment is available. Children can also face discrimination rooted in misconceptions about the condition.

Pinki’s story illustrated how a relatively short procedure can reshape more than a face. After the operation, she was no longer defined solely by her cleft. She returned to her village with a new sense of belonging and eventually stepped onto a global stage, attending the Academy Awards with the film’s team. In 2013, she was invited to perform the ceremonial coin toss before the Wimbledon men’s singles final.

Yet the documentary’s lasting message is not simply about appearance. It is about access — and how poverty can turn a treatable condition into years of social and emotional hardship.

For Pinki, surgery did not erase every challenge of growing up in rural India. But it gave her opportunities that stigma had threatened to take away: the chance to speak, learn, make friends and smile without hiding her face.

Her transformation, captured on film and seen around the world, became a powerful reminder that timely medical care can change the course of a child’s life.

## ‘Smile Pinki’ Oscar Win Shines Spotlight on Cleft Care in India

**LOS ANGELES/NEW DELHI —** *Smile Pinki*, director Megan Mylan’s documentary about an Indian girl receiving surgery for a cleft lip, won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject at the 2009 Oscars, drawing global attention to children living with untreated clefts.

The film follows Pinki Sonkar, a young girl from a poor family in rural Uttar Pradesh. Born with a cleft lip, Pinki faces isolation and is unable to attend school. Her life changes when a social worker identifies her condition and helps her reach a hospital where she receives free corrective surgery.

Mylan, an American documentary filmmaker, focused the film on Pinki’s family and community rather than presenting the story solely as a medical case. The documentary shows both the stigma associated with facial differences and the dramatic effect that access to surgery can have on a child’s confidence and opportunities.

Pinki attended the Academy Awards ceremony with Mylan and became an international symbol of the many children who lack access to cleft treatment. In her acceptance speech, Mylan recognized the medical workers and organizations involved in providing care.

The surgery featured in *Smile Pinki* was supported by Smile Train, an international nonprofit dedicated to cleft treatment. The charity works through local hospitals and medical professionals, funding surgery and supporting services such as speech therapy, dental care, orthodontics and nutritional assistance.

Smile Train’s model emphasizes training and equipping local medical teams so that treatment can be delivered within patients’ own countries and communities. The organization says this approach helps create sustainable systems of care rather than relying primarily on visiting surgical missions.

The Oscar victory gave the charity’s work new visibility while highlighting a broader public-health issue. Cleft lip and palate can affect eating, speaking, hearing and social development, but treatment can significantly improve a patient’s health and quality of life.

More than a portrait of one child, *Smile Pinki* presented Pinki’s transformation as evidence of what timely, accessible care can achieve. Its Academy Award ensured that her story—and the needs of children with untreated clefts—reached audiences around the world.

In Rampur Dabai, a small village in Uttar Pradesh’s Mirzapur district, Pinki Sonkar spent her early childhood marked by a condition she could not control. Born into a poor family with a cleft lip, she was stared at, teased and often kept apart from other children. School—where her appearance might invite more ridicule—seemed beyond her reach.

Her life changed after a social worker connected her family with a program providing free cleft surgery. In 2007, when Pinki was about five years old, plastic surgeon Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh repaired her lip at G.S. Memorial Plastic Surgery Hospital in Varanasi, with support from the international cleft charity Smile Train.

The operation was brief, but its social consequences were profound.

Before surgery, Pinki was shy and reluctant to be seen. Afterward, she began smiling more freely, playing with other children and speaking with greater confidence. The repair did not change who she was; it changed how others responded to her—and helped remove the stigma that had taught her to hide.

That new confidence opened the door to education. Pinki began attending school and participating in ordinary childhood activities that had once seemed inaccessible. Surgery could not erase the poverty and limited opportunities facing her family, but it allowed her to enter the classroom without her cleft being the first thing classmates noticed.

Her relationship with her community shifted as well. A child who had once been treated as different was increasingly welcomed and celebrated. Pinki’s story became widely known through American filmmaker Megan Mylan’s documentary *Smile Pinki*, which followed her journey from isolation to corrective surgery. The film won the 2009 Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject, turning Pinki into an international symbol of the millions of children with treatable clefts.

Her visibility also changed perceptions in her village. Neighbors who had regarded a cleft lip with fear, pity or superstition saw that it was a medical condition that could be repaired. Pinki’s experience encouraged greater awareness among families who might otherwise have hidden children with similar conditions or assumed treatment was unaffordable.

Years later, she appeared on another global stage when she took part in the ceremonial coin toss before the 2013 Wimbledon men’s singles final. Yet the most important change was not the red carpets or public attention. It was the chance to live more comfortably among classmates, neighbors and friends.

Pinki Sonkar’s story is often described as the story of a new smile. More accurately, it is the story of what became possible once a physical difference stopped determining how a child was treated: confidence, schooling, friendship and a recognized place in her community.

# A new smile: Indian girl’s journey from isolation to the Oscars

**MIRZAPUR, India (CNN)** — Born with a cleft lip in a poor village in northern India, Pinki Sonkar spent her early childhood hiding her face and enduring the stares and taunts of other children.

Her family could not afford the operation that would repair the congenital condition. But Pinki’s life changed when a social worker found her in rural Uttar Pradesh and told her parents that she could receive surgery free of charge.

Pinki traveled to a hospital in Varanasi, where plastic surgeon Dr. Subodh Kumar Singh repaired her lip. The relatively brief procedure transformed more than her appearance: It allowed her to eat and speak more easily, attend school with greater confidence and participate more fully in village life.

Her journey became the subject of **“Smile Pinki,”** a short documentary directed by American filmmaker Megan Mylan. The film follows Pinki and her family from their village to the operating room, capturing both the stigma associated with facial differences and the dramatic effect that access to basic medical care can have on a child.

In 2009, when Pinki was 8, the film won the Academy Award for best documentary short subject. Wearing traditional Indian dress, she attended the ceremony in Los Angeles and joined the filmmakers onstage as they accepted the Oscar.

The moment turned a village child who had once been excluded because of her appearance into an international symbol of hope for children born with cleft lips and palates.

Cleft conditions occur when a baby’s lip or the roof of the mouth does not fully form during pregnancy. Without treatment, children may face difficulties eating, speaking and hearing, as well as discrimination and social isolation. Surgery can often repair the condition, but poverty and limited access to specialized care prevent many families from seeking help.

Pinki’s operation was supported through a cleft-treatment program associated with the nonprofit Smile Train. Her story helped draw attention to thousands of children in India and elsewhere who live with a condition that is treatable but can have lifelong consequences when care is unavailable.

For Pinki’s family, however, the transformation was deeply personal. The Oscar brought worldwide attention, but the more meaningful change happened at home: A child who once covered her face could finally smile without fear.
